top.title: 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings
top.summary: A 5,000-year-old mystery surrounding the tombs of Egypt’s first kings has taken a disturbing turn. Scientists reexamining 46 ancient skulls discovered evidence of potentially fatal head injuries in 18, suggesting that at least 39% of those studied may have been deliberately killed. The findings support a century-old theory that royal attendants were sacrificed when kings died, possibly to serve them in the afterlife.

more.summary: Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII, the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program. In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of […]

more.title: Fruit fly sleep protein yields peptides that inhibit drug-resistant bacteria in lab tests
more.summary: Researchers at University of Tsukuba and collaborating institutions have identified short antimicrobial peptides derived from Nemuri, a sleep-inducing protein in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. The research is published in the journal Nature Communications.

more.title: Mountain growth spurts may have sparked complex life on Earth
more.summary: Mountain ranges grew higher throughout Earth's history in two distinct "spurts" that correlated with the flourishing of biological diversity on our planet, according to new research published in the journal Science Advances. The study suggests mountains may have played a key role in sparking complex life.

more.title: Who lives in a sponge under the sea? Tiny Caribbean fish and their microscopic neighbors
more.summary: Two new studies involving Newcastle University marine scientist Dr. Theresa Rueger have highlighted how the tusked goby's relationship with its host sponge shapes almost every aspect of its life. Rueger, a senior lecturer in tropical marine sciences at Newcastle University's School of Natural and Environmental Sciences, is senior author of one study and co-author of the other, which together uncover the influence of…

more.title: Kindergarten teachers offer cognitive help during outdoor play but fall short on emotional and social support
more.summary: A study in the International Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development of teachers' behavior during outdoor play at kindergarten has identified a gap between the support children need and the help educators provide, particularly in emotional and social development.

more.title: A likely supermassive neutron star might shed light on the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes
more.summary: A team of astronomers recently identified a red giant star with an unseen binary companion after examining data from the Large Sky Area MultiObject Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) and the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE). Although the companion object can't be observed visually, astronomers can see the gravitational effects it has on the red giant star.

more.title: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
more.summary: A new study reveals that viral infections may leave behind hidden damage to the immune system long after symptoms disappear. Researchers found that mice recovering from an acute infection experienced lasting changes to their spleens and weakened immune responses, potentially leaving them more vulnerable to future threats. Surprisingly, prior vaccination completely prevented these harmful changes in the mouse model.

more.title: Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains
more.summary: Why do some volcanoes erupt with spectacular lava fountains while others release lava more quietly? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain the difference. Experiments revealed that superheated magma can delay crystal formation for more than eight hours, compared with just 20 minutes in magma that has not been superheated.

more.title: Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps
more.summary: Scientists have captured electrons making seemingly impossible jumps across forbidden energy gaps in graphene, with some transitions occurring at a remarkable 100% probability. The breakthrough offers an unprecedented look at quantum behavior and could help unlock a new generation of ultrafast, light-controlled electronics.

more.title: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago
more.summary: A mysterious force driving the expansion of the Universe may have undergone a dramatic reversal billions of years ago. Scientists exploring an overlooked branch of an alternative gravity theory discovered that dark energy could have switched from negative to positive roughly 9.5 billion years ago, potentially changing how we understand cosmic history.

more.title: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse
more.summary: The massive solar storm that illuminated skies worldwide in May 2024 has uncovered an unexpected twist: Earth's own atmosphere may have helped make the storm so powerful. Satellite measurements revealed that roughly 85% of the charged particles fueling the disturbance originated from Earth's upper atmosphere rather than the solar wind.

more.title: Solar PAC got revenge on clean energy’s enemies in Congress
more.author: Julian Spector
more.summary: Before this election cycle, it was hard to identify any politician who feared the solar industry. The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC set out to change that, and now has a roster of wins to back up its threats. The super PAC, funded and led by solar entrepreneurs and investors, emerged during the midterm primaries…

more.title: The Iran war will cause global fossil fuel emissions to fall
more.author: Dan McCarthy
more.summary: See more from Canary Media’s ​“Chart of the Week” column . Global fossil fuel emissions are expected to dip this year for the first time since 2020. This time it was not plague but war driving the decline. The Iran war has caused brutal increases in oil and natural gas prices, leading many countries to cut their…

more.title: Same farms, different answers: When nitrogen pollution estimates don't add up
more.summary: To reduce nitrogen pollution stemming from synthetic fertilizer and livestock waste, California's Central Valley relies on five data sets to estimate surplus nitrogen. However, most parts of the United States use just one or two data sets—the U.S. Department of Agriculture's agricultural survey and census—to estimate nitrogen surplus.

more.title: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
more.author: Marina Temkin, Dominic-Madori Davis
more.summary: Nvidia poured tens of billions into AI startups under Huang. Without him at the helm, founders and VCs are bracing for smaller checks and lower valuations.

more.title: Hidden 'master switch' allows bacteria to breach the body's defenses
more.summary: Researchers at Penn Dental Medicine have uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism by which bacteria rapidly compromise the body's protective barriers, a finding that could reshape how scientists approach a wide range of serious diseases.

more.title: Modified $450 3D printer builds living materials with more than 100 layers
more.summary: Living materials created with a 3D printer are like living tissues with one notable exception: You get to choose exactly which cells are in them, as well as their final 3D shape. Depending on the type of bacteria included in the print, the material can clean up contaminated water or break down waste materials such as plastic.

more.title: Genomic analysis restores species status to 12 overlooked Great Barrier Reef corals
more.summary: An international team of scientists working with Queensland Museum's CoralBank project has uncovered previously hidden coral diversity on Australia's east coast, revealing that 12 corals once considered variations of other species are distinct species in their own right.

more.title: A perfect couple: Chromium keeps ruthenium grounded in water electrolysis
more.summary: They say opposites attract, and many couples do fit this pattern. One is pragmatic and down-to-earth, while the other is a dreamer with their head in the clouds. Yet, these differences make them perfect for each other. According to researchers at ICFO, chemical interactions between atoms are not that different. Ruthenium, for instance, belongs to the "dreamer" class.

more.title: Crunchbase Data: Nvidia’s Startup Funding Deals Hit A Record. What’s Next After Huang?
more.author: Marlize van Romburgh
more.summary: Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026. We take a fresh look at where Nvidia and its venture arm NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold.

more.title: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
more.author: Jacek Krywko
more.summary: In Sri Lanka, ecological change is shrinking a park's elephant population.
